# Abortion and Breast Cancer Risk: Evidence Assessment

**Conclusion:** The claim that having an abortion increases a woman's risk of breast cancer is not supported by the weight of scientific evidence. Major medical authorities and large-scale analyses have concluded there is no causal link.

## Key Evidence

**1. National Cancer Institute (NCI):** In 2003, the NCI convened a workshop of over 100 leading experts who reviewed population-based, clinical, and animal studies. They concluded that induced abortion does not increase breast cancer risk. The NCI's fact sheet states the scientific evidence does not support a link between abortion and breast cancer.
[https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk](https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk)

**2. American Cancer Society (2023):** States plainly: "the most up-to-date scientific research suggests that abortion does not influence a woman's risk for breast cancer."
[https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html)

**3. Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer (2004):** This major collaborative reanalysis pooled data from 53 epidemiological studies across 16 countries, including 83,000 women with breast cancer. It found no evidence that induced abortion increases breast cancer risk.
[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673604158352](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673604158352)

**4. Updated meta-analysis (2018):** A meta-analysis focusing on prospective evidence did not support a positive association between induced abortion and breast cancer risk.
[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29504989/?dopt=Abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29504989/?dopt=Abstract)

## Why the Claim Persists

Some older case-control studies suggested an association, but these are susceptible to "recall bias"—women with breast cancer may be more likely to report prior abortions than healthy controls. Prospective studies, which avoid this bias, consistently find no link. Sources promoting the claim tend to be advocacy organizations rather than mainstream medical authorities.
